# Phase 2: Strength & Neuromuscular Control {#phase-1-recovery-from-surgery}

```{r setup-root, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
```


At the transition from phase 1 to phase 2, it is expected that pain and swelling have settled down and adequate knee range of motion (ROM) and control have been established. The focus of the rehab can now grow to include building strength and greater neuromuscular control. Key outcomes from Phase 1 will continue to be monitored, including swelling and ROM assessments which remain a part of the criteria. Progressions in both exercise complexity and loading parameters will occur continuously throughout this phase, and it is important that the practitioner monitors these progressions and the athlete's responses carefully. The progressions made in this phase will set the athlete up for more dynamic exercises in Phase 3.

::: {.callout-important title="Most Important Goals — Phase 1"}
-   Rebuild muscular strength, especially the quadriceps and hamstrings
-   Re-establish neuromuscular control (stability, balance, )
-   Listen to the body: be aware of pain, swelling or ROM regressions and adjust training accordingly
:::

Outcomes generally reflect maintaining a healthy knee, increased lower body muscular endurance and strength, and improved balance and stability. **`r params$athlete`'s** progress progress towards these goals will be assessed via the criteria seen below. Detailed description of each criteria and the associated testing methodology can be found in @sec-p2-testing.


## What does the research say? {#sec-p2-research}

### State of the Knee

By satisfying phase 1 criteria before beginning phase 2, we can be confident that the knee is prepared for the increases in load required to build muscular strength. Lingering pain and swelling at this stage will negatively affect joint proprioception @cho2011 and limit neuromuscular activation via the process of arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI)

### Development of Muscular Strength

Perhaps the number one priority during this phase is to restore muscular strength, particularly in the knee extensor muscles @buckthorpe2020.

AMI was discussed at length in Phase 1 \[\], however it continues to play a large part during phase 2 rehab.

Strength training will progress from isolated to functional and from low load to high load. Volume may start in a middle range (to prioritize movement quality over intensity, increase as the body begins to adapt to these movement with the goal of increasing metabolic stress to target muscular strength and hypertrophy, and then volume will begin to decrease as the athlete becomes capable of lifting heavier loads.

### Movement Quality

Movement quality is a broad term involving a number of objective and subjective components. There are certain pieces that can be objectively measured by Phase 2 criteria such as static and dynamic postural stability. There are also important qualities that are difficult to quantify such as optimal kinematics during movement. The ability to judge movement quality in real-time is an important skill for the practitioner to posses.

Mid stage rehab is a period of continuous transition and thus requires intelligent progression. At the start of phase 2, emphasis and attention to detail on movement quality will be high, and loading will be relatively low, and direct loading of the knee joint and affected tissues is carefully progressed. As the athlete progresses through Phase 2,

### OKC

The training program may include both low/no-load full ROM leg extension as well as ROM-restricted leg extension when the patient is able to lift heavier loads. Minimal ACL strain and reduced PFJ reaction forces have been observed during quadriceps contractions performed between 45-90º of knee flexion, and therefore this is the recommended ROM for loading to be introduced @escamilla2012.

Early introduction of isometrics is recommended ?

Leg Ext isometrics between 90-60º (5x45s, 1-2x per day)

Full ROM (90-0º) against gravity/low loads can be performed once able to comfortably achieve 90º knee flexion

Restricted ROM loaded knee extensions may begin 4 weeks post ACLR (Tempo 3:03, 15-25RM loads)

## Testing {#sec-p2-testing}

Each card below contains a detailed description of the tests to be conducted during this phase of rehab.

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}


tests <- criteria_phase2 |>
  dplyr::select(outcome_measure, display_description, additional_information, operator_pretty, goal_pretty, repetitions, calculation, image_path) %>%
  mutate(op_goal = paste(operator_pretty, goal_pretty))

# Helper: print a label/value line only if value is non-missing & non-empty
emit_field <- function(label, value) {
  if (length(value) == 0 || all(is.na(value))) return(invisible())
  val <- value[[1]]
  if (is.na(val)) return(invisible())
  val_chr <- trimws(as.character(val))
  if (!nzchar(val_chr)) return(invisible())
  cat("**", label, ":** ", val_chr, "\n\n", sep = "")
}

#   cat('### ', tests$outcome_measure[i], '\n\n', sep = '')         # heading
#   if (!is.na(tests$display_description[i]) &&
#       nzchar(trimws(tests$display_description[i]))) {
#     cat(tests$display_description[i], '\n\n')
#   }
#   cat("*", tests$additional_information[i], '\n\n')
#   emit_field("Criteria", tests$op_goal[i])                  # always optional-safe
#   emit_field("Repetitions", tests$repetitions[i])                # only prints if present
#   emit_field("Calculation", tests$calculation[i])
# 
#   cat(':::\n\n')
# }

for (i in seq_len(nrow(tests))) {
  cat('::: {.card .ak-card .has-stripe .accent-primary}\n')

  # Use columns instead of layout-columns
  cat('::: {.columns}\n')

  # ---- LEFT: TEXT ----
  cat('::: {.column width="70%"}\n')

  cat('### ', tests$outcome_measure[i], '\n\n', sep = '')

  if (!is.na(tests$display_description[i]) &&
      nzchar(trimws(tests$display_description[i]))) {
    cat(tests$display_description[i], '\n\n')
  }

  cat("*", tests$additional_information[i], '\n\n')

  emit_field("Criteria", tests$op_goal[i])
  emit_field("Repetitions", tests$repetitions[i])
  emit_field("Calculation", tests$calculation[i])

  cat(':::\n')  # end text column

  # ---- RIGHT: IMAGE ----
  cat('::: {.column width="30%"}\n')
  if (!is.na(tests$image_path[i]) && nzchar(trimws(tests$image_path[i]))) {
    cat('![](', tests$image_path[i], '){style="width:100%;"}\n', sep = '')
  }
  cat(':::\n')  # end image column

  cat(':::\n')  # end columns
  cat(':::\n\n')  # end card
}
```

## Additional Resources

### Whole Body Fitness

It is important to distinguish between must-haves and nice-to-haves. For example, development of upper body strength is important however in comparison to something like knee extensor strength, it does not prevent the athlete from progressing the complexity and intensity of rehab @buckthorpe2020.

Another more recent study did not report how early BFR began after surgery, but did use the following criteria to begin BFR: able to stand on one leg unsupported for \>5s, knee ROM between 0-90º, able to perform SLR with sufficient quadriceps activation @barzyk2026 .
